name: Oneleet
tagline: Compliance platform that pairs SOC 2 / ISO 27001 automation with an actual pentest and an audit through a partner firm.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Oneleet quotes annually rather than publishing a monthly number.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build the software half of this: a control checklist, evidence storage, policy docs, and a nag system that tells you which employee has not enabled disk encryption. What you cannot build is the thing you are actually buying, which is a signed attestation from a licensed audit firm plus a penetration test report your prospect's security reviewer will accept. Nobody in procurement wants your self-hosted dashboard screenshot; they want a PDF with an auditor's name on it. The agent-based device monitoring and the read-only cloud integrations are also a long grind of OAuth scopes, endpoint agents for three operating systems, and API drift you get to maintain forever. Build the tracker if you like, but budget for the audit separately, because that is the line item.
coreLoopDIY: A local compliance tracker: define controls, attach evidence files and notes, mark owners and due dates, and export a readiness report showing what is still missing.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine you control
Somewhere private to store evidence files, since they include infra details
Your own reading of the SOC 2 trust services criteria or ISO 27001 Annex A, because the control list is the actual work
A separate budget for a real auditor and a real pentest firm
whatYouLose: The audit itself: no self-hosted tool produces a SOC 2 report a buyer will accept
The bundled penetration test and its report, which is often the reason companies pick Oneleet over pure-automation competitors
Endpoint agents that check disk encryption, screen lock, and OS patch level across macOS, Windows, and Linux fleets
Read-only integrations that pull evidence automatically from AWS, GitHub, Google Workspace, and identity providers instead of you screenshotting things at 1am
A shareable trust page and the vendor-questionnaire answering that comes with a recognized name behind it
moatNotes: The regulated bottleneck is a human CPA firm signing an opinion. Software can only reduce how much of the evidence gathering you do by hand.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the buyer on the other side of the deal does not care how you tracked your controls, they care whether a third party attested to them. Compliance spend is a sales unblocker, not a tooling preference, and the fastest path from "enterprise prospect asked for our SOC 2" to "here is the report" runs through someone who has an auditor relationship and a repeatable evidence pipeline. Add that most engineering teams find compliance work genuinely miserable and will happily pay to have the checklist handed to them with half the boxes pre-filled from their cloud accounts.
notes: The evidence tracker is a weekend build; the attestation is not. The moat is a licensed audit firm's signature plus the buyer-side trust that only that signature buys.
prompt:
Build a local-first compliance readiness tracker called "Readiness". Single user, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, not negotiable:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. No component library.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/readiness.db. Plain SQL in a lib/db.ts module, no ORM.
- Evidence files stored on disk under ./data/evidence/, path recorded in SQLite. Never commit ./data.

Data model:
- framework(id, name)  seed two: "SOC 2 Type II" and "ISO 27001".
- control(id, framework_id, ref, title, description, owner, status, due_date, notes)  status in: not_started, in_progress, ready, not_applicable.
- evidence(id, control_id, filename, original_name, mime, size, captured_on, note).
- policy(id, title, markdown, version, approved_on, owner).

Features, in scope:
1. Controls table with filter by framework, status, and owner. Inline status change.
2. Control detail page: edit fields, upload evidence files (multipart to a route handler, 25MB cap), list evidence with captured_on and a delete button.
3. Staleness flag: any control whose newest evidence is older than 90 days renders a warning badge.
4. Policies section: create and edit markdown policies, bump version, record approved_on and owner. Render markdown read-only view.
5. Readiness report at /report: per-framework percent ready, a table of every control that is not ready or not_applicable, and every stale control. Add a "Print" button that uses print CSS only, no PDF library.
6. Seed script npm run seed that loads a starter control list from data/seed/controls.json. Ship a JSON file with about 25 plausible, clearly generic controls (access review, MFA enforcement, backup restore test, vendor review, incident response drill, onboarding and offboarding checklists). Put a comment in the README that this list is a starting point and not legal or audit advice.

Explicitly out of scope, do not build:
- Endpoint agents, device monitoring, cloud API integrations, OAuth, SSO.
- Multi-tenant anything, invites, roles, audit trails beyond updated_at.
- Any claim of certification. The UI must never use the words "certified" or "compliant", only "ready" and "evidence collected".

Secrets: none needed. Still create .env.example with DATA_DIR and read it in config.
Deliver a README with setup, npm run dev, npm run seed, a backup note (copy ./data), and one blunt paragraph saying this tool tracks readiness and does not produce an audit report, which requires a licensed audit firm.
Include a Vitest file covering the readiness percent calculation and the 90-day staleness rule.
